explanation: Double-quoted strings support variable interpolation and escape sequences (e.g., \n, \t), while single-quoted strings do not, so they are processed differently, not just at different speeds.
The ?? operator is equivalent to isset($var) ? $var : $default, so it does not raise warnings for undefined variables.
The echo statement in PHP accepts multiple comma-separated arguments and concatenates them without a separator.
In PHP, print is a language construct that always returns the integer 1, so it can be used in expressions (unlike echo).
The elvis operator ($a ?: $b) returns the left operand when it is truthy, not falsy; when it is falsy, it returns the right operand.
In PHP, addition/subtraction (+, -) have higher precedence than concatenation (.), so e.g. "1" + 1 . "2" evaluates as ("1"+1) . "2" = "22".
The ** operator is right-associative in PHP, so 2 ** 3 ** 2 evaluates as 2 ** (3 ** 2) = 2 ** 9 = 512, not 64.
The + operator has higher precedence than the . concatenation operator, so it evaluates as 'sum: ' . (2+3) = 'sum: 5'.
With === (strict comparison), arrays must have the same key/value pairs in the same order; it's the loose comparison (==) that ignores order.
In PHP, the loose equality operator == converts false to 0 when compared with an integer, so 0 == 0 is true.
In PHP 8, comparing a non-numeric string to an integer casts the integer to a string, so 'abc' == 0 becomes 'abc' == '0', which is false.
In PHP, null == 0, null == '', and null == false all evaluate to true under loose comparison.
PHP's (int) cast reads the leading numeric portion of the string and stops at the first non-numeric character, so '42abc' becomes 42.
In PHP, the + operator with a numeric string and an integer performs arithmetic addition, converting the string to a number, so '5' + 5 = 10.
In PHP, (string) false results in an empty string "", not "0".
Due to floating-point arithmetic, 0.1 + 0.2 evaluates to 0.30000000000000004, which is not strictly equal to 0.3, so === returns false.
strrev() is byte-oriented, so it reverses individual bytes rather than multi-byte UTF-8 characters, producing an incorrect result for non-ASCII characters.
str_contains('Hello world', 'world') returns true because 'world' is a substring of 'Hello world'.
str_pad() can pad on the right (default), left, or both sides using the STR_PAD_RIGHT, STR_PAD_LEFT, and STR_PAD_BOTH constants.
By default, trim() strips spaces (0x20), tabs (0x09), newlines (0x0A), carriage returns (0x0D), null (0x00), vertical tabs (0x0B), and form feeds (0x0C) from both ends of a string.
In UTF-8, 'é' is 2 bytes, while 'h', 'l', 'l', 'o' are each 1 byte, totaling 6 bytes, which is what strlen() returns.
A negative start position in substr() counts from the end of the string, so -3 returns the last 3 characters.
ucfirst() returns a new string with the first character uppercased; it does not modify the original string in place.
Heredoc (<<<EOF) interpolates variables like double-quoted strings, while nowdoc (<<<'EOF') treats the content as a single-quoted string with no interpolation.
sort() reindexes the array with integer keys; asort() is the function that preserves key-to-value associations.
In PHP, string keys that represent valid integers (like '5') are automatically cast to integer keys when used in arrays.
in_array() uses loose comparison (==) by default; strict mode requires explicitly setting the third parameter to true.
Without a callback, array_filter() internally uses empty() on each element and removes those that evaluate to true (i.e., falsy values like '', 0, '0', null, false, []).
The third parameter $preserve_keys defaults to false, so array_slice() re-indexes keys starting from 0 by default.
array_slice with offset 1 and length 2 extracts elements at indices 1 and 2, which are 20 and 30.
The + operator keeps the left array's value for duplicate keys, so the result is ['a' => 1, 'b' => 2], which has 2 elements.
PHP 8.1 introduced the array spread operator in array literals, which supports both integer and string keys (with later duplicate keys overwriting earlier ones).
Named arguments can be used both before and after ...$args unpacking in a single call, e.g. func(a: 1, ...$args) or func(...$args, a: 1).
In PHP, closures do not automatically capture variables from the outer scope; you must explicitly use the 'use' keyword to import them.
func_num_args() returns the number of arguments actually passed to the function, which is 3 in this case, regardless of the declared parameter count.
An arrow function (fn) body consists of a single expression without curly braces; it implicitly returns that expression.
PHP arrow functions (fn) automatically capture variables from the enclosing scope by value by default, unlike closures which require the `use` keyword.
In PHP, a static closure explicitly does not bind $this, unlike a regular closure which automatically captures it from the enclosing scope.
The use clause captures $x by value (no &), so the closure retains the value 5 even after $x is reassigned to 7.
In weak typing mode (without strict_types=1), PHP will coerce the numeric string "5" to the integer 5 when it matches an int parameter.
Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing properties to be declared directly in constructor parameters with visibility modifiers.
The 'final' keyword in PHP prevents a method from being overridden in subclasses.
In PHP, a method declared with the 'final' keyword cannot be overridden by any subclass, and attempting to do so will result in a fatal error.
Private properties are only accessible within the class that defines them, not in subclasses; only protected and public properties are inherited and accessible in a subclass.
A private parent method is not inherited, so it's not part of the inheritance contract; the child is free to declare a method with the same name at any visibility without conflict.
__get() is called for both inaccessible (private/protected) and undefined (non-existent) properties, not only non-existent ones.
Reassigning a readonly property in PHP throws a ReadOnlyPropertyError, which is a subclass of Error (not Exception).
PHP interfaces can declare constants, which are always public and read-only.
The instanceof operator checks whether an object is an instance of a particular class or implements a particular interface in PHP.
Since PHP 8.0, interfaces can declare static methods with a default implementation.
PHP's instanceof operator checks both class inheritance and interface implementation, so it does not ignore interfaces.
In PHP, interface methods only declare a signature (name, parameters, return type) and cannot have a method body/default implementation, unlike trait methods which can.
In PHP, abstract methods in an abstract class can be declared as public or protected.
Foo::cases() returns an array containing all defined cases of the enum, which are A, B, and C — three elements.
In PHP, both Exception and Error implement the Throwable interface, making it their common ancestor.
TypeError extends LogicException, which extends Exception, so it is caught by catch (Exception $e).
The @ operator suppresses errors, warnings, and notices, but exceptions still propagate normally unless caught by a try-catch block.
intdiv() throws an ArithmeticError when the divisor is zero.
In PHP, the finally block is guaranteed to execute whether or not an exception is caught, including when it propagates up the call stack.
An exception thrown in a finally block replaces (masks) any exception that was being propagated from the try or catch block, so it does affect the result.
Functions registered with register_shutdown_function() are executed during the shutdown phase, which is triggered when exit() or die() is called.
The use statement only creates an alias at compile time; the class file is loaded via autoloading only when the class is actually used (e.g., instantiated or called statically).
In PHP, to import a function from a namespace you use 'use function', while 'use const' is for importing constants.
PSR-4 converts the remaining namespace segments (Controller\Api) into directory paths and the final segment (UserController) into a .php filename, appended to the base directory src/.
Composer's vendor/autoload.php ultimately calls spl_autoload_register() to register the Composer ClassLoader.
__NAMESPACE__ is a magic constant introduced in PHP 5.3 that resolves at compile time to the current namespace name (or an empty string in the global namespace).
An unqualified class name in `new` is resolved relative to the current namespace, not the global root; only a leading backslash forces global root resolution.
PSR-4 maps the namespace App\ to src/, so App\Model\User resolves to src/Model/User.php by replacing remaining namespace separators with directory separators and appending .php.
PHP allows use statements inside a function body, and the alias/import then applies only within that function's scope.
In PHP, arrays are value types and are copied by default on assignment; you must explicitly use the & operator to pass or assign by reference.
PHP arrays are assigned by value (copy-on-write), so modifying $b does not affect $a, which still has 2 elements.
In PHP, variables defined in global scope are not accessible within a function unless you use the global keyword, the $GLOBALS superglobal array, or pass them as parameters.
$GLOBALS['x'] is a reference to the actual global variable, so unset($GLOBALS['x']) removes it globally, not just within the function.
The function increments $n by reference, so $n becomes 6.
A foreach by value iterates over a snapshot of the array taken at the start of the loop, so modifications to the array inside the loop body do not affect the current iteration.
Static properties belong to the class itself and exist in a single shared copy regardless of how many instances are created.
In PHP, boolean array keys are cast to integers (true becomes 1, false becomes 0), so the key is stored as an integer, not a boolean.
Since PHP 7.0, generators can use return with a value, retrievable via $gen->getReturn() after the generator completes.
Generators in PHP are one-shot iterators; once fully consumed, calling rewind() throws an Exception.
yield from (introduced in PHP 7.0) delegates iteration to another generator or iterable, yielding each value from it as if it were part of the current generator.
Calling a generator function returns a Generator object, and get_class() on it returns the string 'Generator'.
The generator yields 3 elements (1, 2, 3), iterator_to_array converts them to an array of 3 elements, and count returns 3.
SplStack implements a LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) stack, not a FIFO queue; SplQueue is the class that implements a FIFO queue.
ArrayIterator is a built-in PHP class that implements the Iterator interface, allowing you to wrap an array and traverse it with foreach or explicit iterator methods.
ArrayObject implements IteratorAggregate, so it can be traversed with foreach.
password_hash() automatically generates a random salt and embeds it in the resulting hash string; no separate salt parameter is needed or accepted.
In PHP 8, PASSWORD_DEFAULT is PASSWORD_ARGON2ID, not md5.
password_verify() returns true when the plaintext password matches the hash, and 'secret' matches its own hash.
strip_tags() removes HTML/PHP tags from a string and is related to XSS protection, but it does not protect against SQL injection, which requires prepared statements or proper escaping.
session_regenerate_id() creates a new session ID while preserving session data, which is the standard defense against session fixation attacks (e.g., after login).
php_sapi_name() is the built-in PHP function that returns the current SAPI module name, such as 'cli', 'fpm-fcgi', or 'apache2handler'.
session_destroy() only destroys the session data on the server; the session cookie in the browser must be manually removed (e.g., with setcookie) to be deleted.
The $_SESSION array is only populated with session data after session_start() is called; without it, the array is empty or undefined.
In PHP, get_class() on an anonymous class returns a string like 'class@anonymous/path:line', and the short form is 'class@anonymous'.
Traits in PHP are allowed to declare constants, properties, and methods.
In PHP, casting any object (including an Exception instance) to bool always returns true, as objects are truthy by definition.
The array_find() function was introduced in PHP 8.3 as part of the new higher-order array functions.
Property hooks (get/set in property declarations) were indeed introduced in PHP 8.4.
Asymmetric visibility (e.g. public private(set)) was indeed introduced in PHP 8.4.
The #[NoDiscard] attribute was introduced in PHP 8.4, allowing developers to mark functions whose return values should not be ignored.
The pipe operator |> has never been a standard PHP operator; the single pipe | is the bitwise OR operator that has existed since PHP 1.0.

The clone-with proposal (clone($obj, ['x' => 1]) to clone with property overrides) was discussed for PHP 8.3, though it was a controversial proposal that many believe was not ultimately accepted into a released version.
array_first() and array_last() were introduced as part of the new array helper functions in PHP 8.3.
The RFC Partial Function Application v2 was adopted for PHP 8.4.
The clamp_v2 RFC was accepted and implemented in PHP 8.4.
The Context Managers v2 RFC (introducing 'using' declarations for automatic resource management) was accepted for inclusion in PHP.
The Generic Types RFC was accepted (for PHP 8.4), not declined.
While ZTS (Zend Thread Safety) is an optional build mode for PHP, no RFC has been adopted to make it the default; PHP still ships as NTS (Non-Thread Safe) by default.
PHP 8.5 does not include native generics (parameterized types); developers still rely on @template docblock annotations for static analysis tools only.
PHP releases follow a ~6-month cycle on the third Thursday of November; PHP 8.5 went GA in November 2025, and PHP 8.6 is scheduled for November 19, 2026, making it unreleased as of November 6, 2026.
PHP 6 was in development for years but never released; PHP 7.0 (December 2015) followed directly after PHP 5.6 (November 2014) as the next major version.
The RFC for a #[\Deprecated] attribute was proposed but not adopted into PHP core.
